Objective vs. Search: Decomposing What Makes a Good Tokeniser

Ahmetcan Yavuz Affiliation: ETH Zürich    Clara Meister Affiliation: EPFL    Tiago Pimentel Email: ayavuz@ethz.ch,  clara.meister@epfl.ch,  tiago.pimentel@inf.ethz.ch
Ahmetcanyvz/comp-vs-like & Ahmetcanyvz/comp-vs-like
Affiliation: ETH Zürich
Abstract

Two dominant tokenisation algorithms are used by modern language models: byte-pair encoding (BPE) and UnigramLM. These differ along two orthogonal axes: their optimisation objective (compression vs. log-likelihood) and their search procedure (bottom-up merging vs. top-down pruning). Existing comparisons confound these axes, making it unclear whether their observed differences stem from what is being optimised vs. how it is being optimised. We disentangle the two by introducing two new tokenisation algorithms that complete this 2×\times2 design space: BottomUpLL, a bottom-up likelihood-based tokeniser, and TopDownComp, a top-down compression-based tokeniser. We train language models with tokenisers produced by each algorithm, varying: model size, vocabulary sizes, and domain (English-only vs. multilingual). Evaluating models on bits-per-byte, we find that the search procedure—not the objective—is the dominant factor: bottom-up tokenisers consistently achieve lower bits-per-byte in most settings. Evaluating models on the BLiMP task, however, shows no consistent relationship between design choice and performance. Overall, our results disentangle the effect of tokeniser design choices on language modelling performance, offering concrete guidance for their more principled construction.

1 Introduction

Before a language model (LM) processes text, its raw character string is mapped to a token string, which defines the model’s input. This mapping is performed by a tokeniser, a foundational component of modern language modelling pipelines, used in virtually all state-of-the-art models (Team, 2026; OpenAI et al., 2025; Team et al., 2026). A tokeniser is defined by several attributes. Some, such as the vocabulary size, are set by the practitioner while others, such as the vocabulary itself, are learned from data by a tokeniser learning algorithm. Two such algorithms account for most tokenisers in current use: (i) byte-pair encoding (BPE), which learns a vocabulary that maximises the compression of a training corpus (Gage, 1994; Sennrich et al., 2016); and (ii) UnigramLM, which learns a vocabulary that maximises the unigram log-likelihood of a training corpus (Kudo, 2018).

Despite their widespread usage, though, it remains unclear what makes a good tokeniser. BPE and UnigramLM are used as the default algorithms; yet their design choices have received little direct examination, and upon closer inspection, confound many of the existing comparisons. As a concrete example, the results of Schmidt et al. (2024)—that language models trained with BPE often perform better than those trained with UnigramLM—are commonly read as evidence that compression is a better optimisation objective than unigram log-likelihood. Optimisation objectives, though, are only one facet of a tokeniser learning algorithm.

BPE and UnigramLM also differ in the search procedure used to maximize the objective.11 1 The optimisation problem that such algorithms must solve is, in general, NP-hard (Kozma and Voderholzer, 2024; Whittington et al., 2025; Kastreva et al., 2026), so tokeniser learning algorithms typically approximate a solution with a heuristic search procedure. Given a dataset, BPE uses a bottom-up search, greedily merging symbols to maximise compression. UnigramLM relies on a top-down search, starting from an oversized vocabulary and iteratively pruning tokens to maximise log-likelihood. BPE and UnigramLM therefore differ along two axes at once: the optimisation objective and the search procedure. A comparison between the two cannot attribute the difference in performance to either axis alone.

In this work, we disentangle these two axes. We introduce BottomUpLL, a bottom-up likelihood-based tokeniser that mirrors BPE’s merge procedure but optimises corpus log-likelihood instead of compression. We also introduce TopDownComp, a top-down compression-based tokeniser that follows UnigramLM’s pruning procedure but optimises compression. Together with BPE and UnigramLM, these methods form a 2×22\times 2 study crossing objective (compression vs. log-likelihood) and search procedure (bottom-up vs. top-down); see Fig. 1.

We train language models with tokenisers produced by all four algorithms, evaluating them in English-only and multilingual settings. We analyse these models with a combination of extrinsic and intrinsic evaluations. Notably, our results show that search procedure has a stronger influence on bits-per-byte (BPB) than the training objective, with bottom-up tokenisers achieving the best BPB scores in nearly all experimental conditions (BPE outperforms TopDownComp, and BottomUpLL outperforms UnigramLM). This ordering does not carry over to grammaticality judgements (on a BLiMP task), though, where neither the objective nor the search procedure separates the tokenisers consistently. Interestingly, at small vocabulary settings, however, the objective still matters, with likelihood-based tokenisers outperform compression-based ones. Overall, our results highlight the importance of both optimisation objective and search procedure to tokeniser training algorithm design.

2 Tokenisation

Language modelling starts from raw text, which can be represented as character-strings 𝐜∈Σ∗{\color[rgb]{0.2734,0.4688,1}\mathbf{c}}\in{\color[rgb]{0.2734,0.4688,1}\Sigma}^{*}; these are finite sequences of characters 𝐜=c1​c2​…​c|𝐜|{\color[rgb]{0.2734,0.4688,1}\mathbf{c}}={\color[rgb]{0.2734,0.4688,1}{\color[rgb]{0.2734,0.4688,1}c}_{1}{\color[rgb]{0.2734,0.4688,1}c}_{2}\dots{\color[rgb]{0.2734,0.4688,1}c}_{|{\color[rgb]{0.2734,0.4688,1}\mathbf{c}}|}} over alphabet Σ{\color[rgb]{0.2734,0.4688,1}\Sigma}.22 2 As usual, Σ∗{\color[rgb]{0.2734,0.4688,1}\Sigma}^{*} denotes the Kleene star of Σ{\color[rgb]{0.2734,0.4688,1}\Sigma}, while Σ+{\color[rgb]{0.2734,0.4688,1}\Sigma}^{+} denotes the set of all non-empty strings over Σ{\color[rgb]{0.2734,0.4688,1}\Sigma}. A tokeniser’s job is then to segment these character-strings into token-strings 𝐬∈𝒮∗{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}\mathbf{s}}\in{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}\mathcal{S}}^{*}: sequences 𝐬=⟨s1,s2,…,s|𝐬|⟩{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}\mathbf{s}}={\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}\langle{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s_{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}1}}},{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s_{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}2}}},\dots,{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s_{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}|{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}\mathbf{s}}|}}}\rangle}, where each symbol st{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s_{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}t}}} is called a token and represents a non-empty character span. Whenever 𝐬{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}\mathbf{s}} is a segmentation of 𝐜{\color[rgb]{0.2734,0.4688,1}\mathbf{c}}, we say these strings are equivalent, which we denote as 𝐜​=∘​𝐬{\color[rgb]{0.2734,0.4688,1}\mathbf{c}}\overset{\circ}{=}{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}\mathbf{s}}, i.e.:33 3 We restrict our discussion to lossless tokenisers here.

𝐜​=∘​𝐬⇔𝐜=s1∘s2∘⋯∘s|𝐬|,\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{0.2734,0.4688,1}\mathbf{c}}\overset{\circ}{=}{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}\mathbf{s}}\iff{\color[rgb]{0.2734,0.4688,1}\mathbf{c}}={\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s_{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}1}}}\circ{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s_{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}2}}}\circ\dots\circ{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s_{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}|{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}\mathbf{s}}|}}}, (1)

Notably, tokenisers are usually not allowed to output any possible segmentation of 𝐜{\color[rgb]{0.2734,0.4688,1}\mathbf{c}}, being instead constrained to segment it using only the tokens in a finite set called its vocabulary 𝒮⊂Σ+{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}\mathcal{S}}\subset{\color[rgb]{0.2734,0.4688,1}\Sigma}^{+}. To ensure that any character-string can be represented as tokens, we enforce Σ⊆𝒮{\color[rgb]{0.2734,0.4688,1}\Sigma}\subseteq{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}\mathcal{S}}.

How do we convert between character- and token-strings, though? Given just a vocabulary 𝒮{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}\mathcal{S}}, there are multiple different ways a character-string could be mapped to items in that vocabulary. For example, if 𝒮={a,a​a,a​a​a},{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}\mathcal{S}}=\{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}a},{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}aa},{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}aaa}\}, then the character-string 𝐜=a​a​a{\color[rgb]{0.2734,0.4688,1}\mathbf{c}}={\color[rgb]{0.2734,0.4688,1}aaa} may be encoded as either ⟨a,a​a⟩{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}\langle a,aa\rangle}, ⟨a​a,a⟩{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}\langle aa,a\rangle}, or ⟨a,a,a⟩{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}\langle a,a,a\rangle}, which we refer to as segmentations. Consequently, a tokeniser is defined not only by its vocabulary, but also by how it maps character-strings to segmentations. This mapping is the job of an encoding function, 𝚝𝚘𝚔:Σ∗→𝒮∗{\color[rgb]{1,0.4688,0.0781}\mathtt{tok}}:{\color[rgb]{0.2734,0.4688,1}\Sigma}^{*}\to{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}\mathcal{S}}^{*}, which segments the original character-string into tokens; by definition, we have thus that 𝐜​=∘​𝚝𝚘𝚔​(𝐜){\color[rgb]{0.2734,0.4688,1}\mathbf{c}}\overset{\circ}{=}{\color[rgb]{1,0.4688,0.0781}\mathtt{tok}}({\color[rgb]{0.2734,0.4688,1}\mathbf{c}}). Finally, a tokeniser also contains a decoding function, 𝚍𝚎𝚝𝚘𝚔:𝒮∗→Σ∗{\color[rgb]{1,0.4688,0.0781}\mathtt{detok}}:{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}\mathcal{S}}^{*}\to{\color[rgb]{0.2734,0.4688,1}\Sigma}^{*}, which converts token-strings back into characters, being typically defined as the concatenation of each token’s characters: 𝚍𝚎𝚝𝚘𝚔⁡(𝐬)=defs1∘s2∘⋯∘s|𝐬|{\color[rgb]{1,0.4688,0.0781}\mathtt{detok}}({\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}\mathbf{s}})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\texttt{def}}}{{=}}{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s_{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}1}}}\circ{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s_{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}2}}}\circ\dots\circ{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s_{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}|{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}\mathbf{s}}|}}}. Formally, we thus define a tokeniser as the tuple 𝕋=def⟨𝒮,𝚍𝚎𝚝𝚘𝚔,𝚝𝚘𝚔⟩{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}\mathbb{T}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\texttt{def}}}{{=}}\langle{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}\mathcal{S}},{\color[rgb]{1,0.4688,0.0781}\mathtt{detok}},{\color[rgb]{1,0.4688,0.0781}\mathtt{tok}}\rangle.

3 Learning a Tokeniser: Optimisation Objective vs. Search Procedure

How do we select such a tokeniser? Here, we cast the learning of a tokeniser as the combination of two design components: an objective function and a search procedure.

3.1 Objective Functions

Given a tokeniser 𝕋{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}\mathbb{T}} and a dataset 𝒟={𝐜m}m=1M\mathcal{D}=\{{\color[rgb]{0.2734,0.4688,1}\mathbf{c}}_{m}\}_{m=1}^{M}, an objective function 𝔊{\color[rgb]{1,0.4688,0.0781}\mathfrak{G}} assigns a score to the tokeniser. Different objectives encode different notions of what makes a tokeniser useful. We focus on two standard objectives used by tokeniser learning algorithms: compression and log-likelihood.

Under the compression objective, the quantity to be minimised is the total number of tokens that the tokeniser produces on the dataset:

𝔊comp​(𝚝𝚘𝚔,𝒟)=def∑𝐜∈𝒟|𝚝𝚘𝚔⁡(𝐜)|,\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{1,0.4688,0.0781}\mathfrak{G}}_{\mathrm{comp}}({\color[rgb]{1,0.4688,0.0781}\mathtt{tok}},\mathcal{D})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\texttt{def}}}{{=}}\sum_{{\color[rgb]{0.2734,0.4688,1}\mathbf{c}}\in\mathcal{D}}|{\color[rgb]{1,0.4688,0.0781}\mathtt{tok}}({\color[rgb]{0.2734,0.4688,1}\mathbf{c}})|, (2)

This is appealing because shorter token strings improve effective context usage and reduce the number of model steps needed to process a dataset.

Under the log-likelihood objective, the minimised quantity is the negative log-probability that a given probabilistic model p𝜽p_{\bm{\theta}} assigns the corpus:

𝔊ll(𝚝𝚘𝚔,𝒟)=def−∑𝐜∈𝒟logp𝜽(𝚝𝚘𝚔(𝐜)).\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{1,0.4688,0.0781}\mathfrak{G}}_{\mathrm{ll}}({\color[rgb]{1,0.4688,0.0781}\mathtt{tok}},\mathcal{D})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\texttt{def}}}{{=}}-\sum_{{\color[rgb]{0.2734,0.4688,1}\mathbf{c}}\in\mathcal{D}}\log p_{\bm{\theta}}\bigl({\color[rgb]{1,0.4688,0.0781}\mathtt{tok}}({\color[rgb]{0.2734,0.4688,1}\mathbf{c}})\bigr). (3)

where p𝜽p_{\bm{\theta}}’s parameters 𝜽\bm{\theta} are themselves optimised to model this tokeniser’s text. This objective is likewise appealing, since log-likelihood is also the training objective of the language models for which these tokenisers are designed—so a log-likelihood optimal tokeniser would, by construction, lead to better models. Optimising log-likelihood directly, however, is intractable, as this objective requires fully training language models p𝜽p_{\bm{\theta}} for its evaluation.

In practice, to make this objective tractable, we typically significantly restrict the class of models p𝜽p_{\bm{\theta}}. Here, we follow UnigramLM in restricting p𝜽p_{\bm{\theta}} to unigram language models. For a fixed encoding function 𝚝𝚘𝚔{\color[rgb]{1,0.4688,0.0781}\mathtt{tok}}, let nsDn_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}}^{{\lx@scalerel@obj{\mathcal{D}}}} denote the count of token s{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s} in the tokenised corpus, and let ND=def∑s∈𝒮nsDN^{\lx@scalerel@obj{\mathcal{D}}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\texttt{def}}}{{=}}\sum_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}\in{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}\mathcal{S}}}n_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}}^{{\lx@scalerel@obj{\mathcal{D}}}} be the total number of tokens. We then define p𝜽p_{\bm{\theta}} as

p𝜽​(𝐬)=∏t=1|𝐬|p𝜽​(st),p𝜽​(s)=nsDND.p_{\bm{\theta}}({\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}\mathbf{s}})=\prod_{t=1}^{|{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}\mathbf{s}}|}p_{\bm{\theta}}({\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s_{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}t}}}),\qquad p_{\bm{\theta}}({\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s})=\frac{n_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}}^{{\lx@scalerel@obj{\mathcal{D}}}}}{N^{\lx@scalerel@obj{\mathcal{D}}}}. (4)

Concretely, we will thus use unigram log-likelihood as the objective here, as opposed to ‘full’ log-likelihood, and, for the rest of this paper, log-likelihood stands for unigram log-likelihood.

3.2 Search Procedures

Given one of these objectives and a fixed vocabulary budget KK, we might expect a tokeniser to be chosen by directly optimising

𝚝𝚘𝚔𝚘𝚙𝚝=argmin𝚝𝚘𝚔∈𝒯K𝔊​(𝚝𝚘𝚔,𝒟),\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{1,0.4688,0.0781}\mathtt{tok}}_{\mathtt{opt}}=\argmin_{{\color[rgb]{1,0.4688,0.0781}\mathtt{tok}}\in\mathcal{T}_{K}}{\color[rgb]{1,0.4688,0.0781}\mathfrak{G}}({\color[rgb]{1,0.4688,0.0781}\mathtt{tok}},\mathcal{D}), (5)

where 𝒯K\mathcal{T}_{K} denotes whichever class of tokenisers is under consideration. Unfortunately, this optimisation problem is computationally intractable; the compression variant is provably NP-hard (Kozma and Voderholzer, 2024; Whittington et al., 2025; Kastreva et al., 2026), and we suspect the log-likelihood variant to be as well. In practice, heuristic search procedures are therefore required. Such procedures specify both a restricted class of tokenisers and a strategy for selecting an element from that class. We focus on two standard search procedures: bottom-up construction and top-down pruning.

The bottom-up procedure builds a tokeniser from the bottom up: the vocabulary starts as the alphabet Σ{\color[rgb]{0.2734,0.4688,1}\Sigma} and grows one token at a time through merge operations. Given a merge m=⟨s′,s′′⟩{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}m}=\langle{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{\prime},{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{\prime\prime}\rangle, applying it to a token-string rewrites every (non-overlapping) occurrence of bigram s′,s′′{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{\prime},{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{\prime\prime} into the token snew=s′∘s′′{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{\texttt{new}}={\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{\prime}\circ{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{\prime\prime}. A merge list 𝐦=m1,…,mk{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}\mathbf{m}}={\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}m}_{1},\dots,{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}m}_{k} then defines an encoding function 𝚝𝚘𝚔↑​[𝐦]{\color[rgb]{1,0.4688,0.0781}\mathtt{tok}_{\uparrow}}[{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}\mathbf{m}}]: starting from 𝐜{\color[rgb]{0.2734,0.4688,1}\mathbf{c}} as a token-string over Σ{\color[rgb]{0.2734,0.4688,1}\Sigma} (one token per character), it applies m1,…,mk{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}m}_{1},\dots,{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}m}_{k} in order. The final token-string is our tokenised text. We write the tokeniser class defined by this procedure as 𝒯K↑={𝚝𝚘𝚔↑​[𝐦]∣𝐦∈(Σ+×Σ+)K}\mathcal{T}_{K}^{\uparrow}=\bigl\{{\color[rgb]{1,0.4688,0.0781}\mathtt{tok}_{\uparrow}}[{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}\mathbf{m}}]\mid{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}\mathbf{m}}\in({\color[rgb]{0.2734,0.4688,1}\Sigma}^{+}\times{\color[rgb]{0.2734,0.4688,1}\Sigma}^{+})^{K}\bigr\}. To select an element from this class, we then start from an empty merge list, and greedily add one merge per step to it, locally optimising an objective 𝔊{\color[rgb]{1,0.4688,0.0781}\mathfrak{G}}:

m⋆=argminm∈Σ+×Σ+𝔊​(𝚝𝚘𝚔↑​[𝐦<k,m],𝒟),\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}m}^{\star}=\argmin_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}m}\in{\color[rgb]{0.2734,0.4688,1}\Sigma}^{+}\times{\color[rgb]{0.2734,0.4688,1}\Sigma}^{+}}{\color[rgb]{1,0.4688,0.0781}\mathfrak{G}}({\color[rgb]{1,0.4688,0.0781}\mathtt{tok}_{\uparrow}}[{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}\mathbf{m}}_{<k},{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}m}],\mathcal{D}), (6)

where 𝚝𝚘𝚔↑​[𝐦<k,m]{\color[rgb]{1,0.4688,0.0781}\mathtt{tok}_{\uparrow}}[{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}\mathbf{m}}_{<k},{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}m}] denotes the encoding function obtained by applying the current merge list 𝐦<k{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}\mathbf{m}}_{<k} followed by the candidate m{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}m}. The selected merge m⋆{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}m}^{\star} is then appended to the merge list. We refer to a candidate merge’s effect on the objective as its merge gain, and write it Δs1,s2𝔊⁡(⋅,𝒟)\Delta_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{1},{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{2}}^{{\color[rgb]{1,0.4688,0.0781}\mathfrak{G}}(\cdot,\mathcal{D})}.

By contrast, the top-down procedure starts from a large candidate vocabulary 𝒮0{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}\mathcal{S}}_{0}, with |𝒮0|≫K|{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}\mathcal{S}}_{0}|\gg K, and removes tokens until |𝒮|=|Σ|+K|{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}\mathcal{S}}|=|{\color[rgb]{0.2734,0.4688,1}\Sigma}|+K. Notably, this procedure does not rely on merge lists, but instead commits to an objective-optimal encoding function 𝚝𝚘𝚔⇒​[𝒮]{\color[rgb]{1,0.4688,0.0781}\mathtt{tok}_{\Rightarrow}}[{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}\mathcal{S}}], determined by the vocabulary alone. Under compression, 𝚝𝚘𝚔⇒​[𝒮]​(𝐜){\color[rgb]{1,0.4688,0.0781}\mathtt{tok}_{\Rightarrow}}[{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}\mathcal{S}}]({\color[rgb]{0.2734,0.4688,1}\mathbf{c}}) is the shortest valid segmentation of 𝐜{\color[rgb]{0.2734,0.4688,1}\mathbf{c}} using tokens from 𝒮{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}\mathcal{S}}. Under log-likelihood, it is instead the most probable segmentation of 𝐜{\color[rgb]{0.2734,0.4688,1}\mathbf{c}} under p𝜽p_{\bm{\theta}}.44 4 Given a fixed p𝜽p_{\bm{\theta}}, both cases can be computed efficiently. For log-likelihood, however, the parameters of p𝜽p_{\bm{\theta}} itself depend on 𝚝𝚘𝚔{\color[rgb]{1,0.4688,0.0781}\mathtt{tok}}, creating a circular definition. In practice, the two are estimated jointly as we explain in § 4.2. Top-down’s tokeniser class can then be written as: 𝒯K↓={𝚝𝚘𝚔⇒[𝒮]∣𝒮⊂Σ+,Σ⊆𝒮,|𝒮|=|Σ|+K}\mathcal{T}_{K}^{\downarrow}=\bigl\{{\color[rgb]{1,0.4688,0.0781}\mathtt{tok}_{\Rightarrow}}[{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}\mathcal{S}}]\mid{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}\mathcal{S}}\subset{\color[rgb]{0.2734,0.4688,1}\Sigma}^{+},{\color[rgb]{0.2734,0.4688,1}\Sigma}\subseteq{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}\mathcal{S}},|{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}\mathcal{S}}|=|{\color[rgb]{0.2734,0.4688,1}\Sigma}|+K\bigr\}. To select an item in this class, we then start from a large vocabulary 𝒮0{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}\mathcal{S}}_{0}, from which we iteratively prune the least critical tokens, quantified as the tokens whose removal has the least negative impact on the objective we’re optimizing for:

s✗=argmins∈𝒮k−1∖Σ𝔊​(𝚝𝚘𝚔⇒​[𝒮k−1∖{s}],𝒟).\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}_{\text{✗}}=\argmin_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}\in{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}\mathcal{S}}_{k-1}\setminus{\color[rgb]{0.2734,0.4688,1}\Sigma}}{\color[rgb]{1,0.4688,0.0781}\mathfrak{G}}({\color[rgb]{1,0.4688,0.0781}\mathtt{tok}_{\Rightarrow}}[{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}\mathcal{S}}_{k-1}\setminus\{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}\}],\mathcal{D}). (7)

Here, we index pruning steps by kk, mirroring the bottom-up case. This yields 𝒮k=𝒮k−1∖{s✗}{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}\mathcal{S}}_{k}={\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}\mathcal{S}}_{k-1}\setminus\{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}_{\text{✗}}\}. Importantly, to ensure every string remains encodable, alphabet tokens are never removed; pruning then continues until |𝒮|=|Σ|+K|{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}\mathcal{S}}|=|{\color[rgb]{0.2734,0.4688,1}\Sigma}|+K.55 5 We note that, for efficiency reasons, in practice, multiple tokens are often pruned in batches. Analogously, we refer to a candidate deletion’s effect on the objective as its deletion cost, written Δs𝔊⁡(⋅,𝒟)\Delta_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}}^{{\color[rgb]{1,0.4688,0.0781}\mathfrak{G}}(\cdot,\mathcal{D})}.

4 Analysed Tokenisers: Old and New

Combining the objectives and search procedures above, we get a 2×22\times 2 design space for tokenisation algorithms (illustrated in Fig. 1). Existing tokeniser learning algorithms, namely BPE and UnigramLM, cover only two of these cells. Here, we introduce algorithms that instantiate the two other cells: BottomUpLL, a bottom-up likelihood-based method, and TopDownComp, a top-down compression-based method.66 6 Our new methods are closely related to, e.g., WordPiece or PathPiece. We discuss this prior work in detail in § 5. Before any of these methods can be run, however, a loose end remains.

In the previous section, we describe the search procedures as greedy: at each step, it picks the merge m⋆{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}m}^{\star} or deletion s✗{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}_{\text{✗}} which (locally) optimises an objective 𝔊⁡(⋅,𝒟){\color[rgb]{1,0.4688,0.0781}\mathfrak{G}}(\cdot,\mathcal{D}). It did not specify, however, how this selection is performed. Taken literally, computing the argmin\argmin operations in Eqs. 6 and 7 would require running the objective function 𝔊{\color[rgb]{1,0.4688,0.0781}\mathfrak{G}} once per candidate to find the optimal one—a computationally impractical operation. Rather than recomputing 𝔊{\color[rgb]{1,0.4688,0.0781}\mathfrak{G}} every time, most tokenisation algorithms work with incremental scores instead:

m⋆\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}m}^{\star} =argmax⟨s1,s2⟩∈Σ+×Σ+Δs1,s2𝔊⁡(⋅,𝒟)\displaystyle=\argmax_{\langle{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{1},{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{2}\rangle\in{\color[rgb]{0.2734,0.4688,1}\Sigma}^{+}\times{\color[rgb]{0.2734,0.4688,1}\Sigma}^{+}}\Delta_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{1},{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{2}}^{{\color[rgb]{1,0.4688,0.0781}\mathfrak{G}}(\cdot,\mathcal{D})} (8a)
s✗\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}_{\text{✗}} =argmins∈𝒮k−1∖ΣΔs𝔊⁡(⋅,𝒟)\displaystyle=\,\,\,\,\,\,\argmin_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}\in{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}\mathcal{S}}_{k-1}\setminus{\color[rgb]{0.2734,0.4688,1}\Sigma}}\,\,\,\,\,\,\Delta_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}}^{{\color[rgb]{1,0.4688,0.0781}\mathfrak{G}}(\cdot,\mathcal{D})} (8b)

Notably, these equations are equivalent to § 3.2’s, as the pre-update objective values (e.g., 𝔊⁡(𝚝𝚘𝚔↑​[𝐦<k],𝒟){\color[rgb]{1,0.4688,0.0781}\mathfrak{G}}({\color[rgb]{1,0.4688,0.0781}\mathtt{tok}_{\uparrow}}[{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}\mathbf{m}}_{<k}],\mathcal{D})) do not depend on the candidates, and are thus constant. Each search procedure then derives a way to compute (or approximate) these values efficiently, as we show next.

4.1 Bottom-up tokenisers: BPE and BottomUpLL

For a bottom-up method, each candidate is scored according to its merge gain Δs1,s2𝔊⁡(⋅,𝒟)\Delta_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{1},{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{2}}^{{\color[rgb]{1,0.4688,0.0781}\mathfrak{G}}(\cdot,\mathcal{D})}. We now show how this score can be computed efficiently for the two objectives, starting with compression.

Lemma 1.

The change in compression due to merging a token-pair can be computed as:

Δs1,s2𝔊comp​(⋅,𝒟)=ns1,s2D\displaystyle\Delta_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{1},{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{2}}^{{\color[rgb]{1,0.4688,0.0781}\mathfrak{G}}_{\mathrm{comp}}(\cdot,\mathcal{D})}=n_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{1},{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{2}}^{{\lx@scalerel@obj{\mathcal{D}}}} (9)

where ns1,s2Dn_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{1},{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{2}}^{{\lx@scalerel@obj{\mathcal{D}}}} denotes the number of non-overlapping ⟨s1,s2⟩\langle{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{1},{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{2}\rangle sequences in 𝒟\mathcal{D}.

Proof sketch.

The full proof is in Appendix A. Replacing an occurrence of the token-pair m=⟨s1,s2⟩{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}m}=\langle{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{1},{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{2}\rangle with the merged token s1∘s2{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{1}\circ{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{2} saves one token. Further, the number of non-overlapping occurrences of a token-pair is its number of possible merges. Merging the pair therefore shortens the corpus by exactly ns1,s2Dn_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{1},{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{2}}^{{\lx@scalerel@obj{\mathcal{D}}}} tokens, which is its gain under 𝔊comp{\color[rgb]{1,0.4688,0.0781}\mathfrak{G}}_{\mathrm{comp}}. ∎

Lemma 1 gives the standard BPE merge rule: the compression-optimal merge is the most (non-overlappingly) frequent token-pair. In practice, the token-pair counts ns1,s2Dn_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{1},{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{2}}^{{\lx@scalerel@obj{\mathcal{D}}}} are computed once and then updated incrementally after each merge, rather than recomputed from scratch (see App. B), which allows us to run BPE efficiently. We can derive an analogous equivalence for BottomUpLL.

The change in log-likelihood due to merging a token-pair can be computed as:77 7 For the case s1=s2{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{1}={\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{2}, the same calculation applies albeit with a modified count update: each merge consumes two occurrences of the same token s1{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{1} and thus its count is reduced by 2​ns1,s1D2n_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{1},{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{1}}^{{\lx@scalerel@obj{\mathcal{D}}}} instead; other parts of the update remain unchanged.

Δs1,s2𝔊ll​(⋅,𝒟)=\displaystyle\Delta_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{1},{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{2}}^{{\color[rgb]{1,0.4688,0.0781}\mathfrak{G}}_{\mathrm{ll}}(\cdot,\mathcal{D})}\!= (10)
(ns1D−ns1,s2D)​log⁡(ns1D−ns1,s2D)−ns1D​log⁡ns1D\displaystyle\,\,(n_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{1}}^{{\lx@scalerel@obj{\mathcal{D}}}}-n_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{1},{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{2}}^{{\lx@scalerel@obj{\mathcal{D}}}})\log(n_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{1}}^{{\lx@scalerel@obj{\mathcal{D}}}}-n_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{1},{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{2}}^{{\lx@scalerel@obj{\mathcal{D}}}})-n_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{1}}^{{\lx@scalerel@obj{\mathcal{D}}}}\log n_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{1}}^{{\lx@scalerel@obj{\mathcal{D}}}}
+(ns2D−ns1,s2D)​log⁡(ns2D−ns1,s2D)−ns2D​log⁡ns2D\displaystyle\,\,+(n_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{2}}^{{\lx@scalerel@obj{\mathcal{D}}}}-n_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{1},{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{2}}^{{\lx@scalerel@obj{\mathcal{D}}}})\log(n_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{2}}^{{\lx@scalerel@obj{\mathcal{D}}}}-n_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{1},{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{2}}^{{\lx@scalerel@obj{\mathcal{D}}}})-n_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{2}}^{{\lx@scalerel@obj{\mathcal{D}}}}\log n_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{2}}^{{\lx@scalerel@obj{\mathcal{D}}}}
+ns1,s2D​log⁡ns1,s2D\displaystyle\,\,+n_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{1},{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{2}}^{{\lx@scalerel@obj{\mathcal{D}}}}\log n_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{1},{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{2}}^{{\lx@scalerel@obj{\mathcal{D}}}}

Proof sketch.

The full proof is in Appendix C. Note that, if a token changes from count n1n_{1} to count n2n_{2}, its contribution to the log-likelihood objective changes by: n2​log⁡n2−n1​log⁡n1n_{2}\log n_{2}-n_{1}\log n_{1}. The lemma then follows trivially, noting that: (i) the old tokens s1{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{1} and s2{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{2} change from, e.g., frequency ns1Dn_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{1}}^{{\lx@scalerel@obj{\mathcal{D}}}} to (ns1D−ns1,s2D)(n_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{1}}^{{\lx@scalerel@obj{\mathcal{D}}}}-n_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{1},{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{2}}^{{\lx@scalerel@obj{\mathcal{D}}}}); (ii) the new token s1∘s2{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{1}\circ{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{2} changes from frequency 0 to ns1,s2Dn_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{1},{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{2}}^{{\lx@scalerel@obj{\mathcal{D}}}}. Further, the total count of tokens serves as a normalisation factor in all tokens, and thus enters the log-likelihood with the opposite sign; its contribution changes from NDN^{\lx@scalerel@obj{\mathcal{D}}} to ND−ns1,s2DN^{\lx@scalerel@obj{\mathcal{D}}}-n_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{1},{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{2}}^{{\lx@scalerel@obj{\mathcal{D}}}}. ∎

BottomUpLL can thus also be implemented efficiently, maintaining local count statistics and updating only affected candidate scores after each merge. Interestingly, an analysis of the merge gain definition in Lemma 2 shows that, for a token-pair to be selected: (i) the pair should occur often enough to matter, but (ii) it should also be favoured when its tokens co-occur more systematically than expected from their individual frequencies.

4.2 Top-down tokenisers: UnigramLM and TopDownComp

For top-down methods, each candidate’s score is given by the deletion cost Δs𝔊⁡(⋅,𝒟)\Delta_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}}^{{\color[rgb]{1,0.4688,0.0781}\mathfrak{G}}(\cdot,\mathcal{D})}. Unfortunately, this cost Δs𝔊⁡(⋅,𝒟)\Delta_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}}^{{\color[rgb]{1,0.4688,0.0781}\mathfrak{G}}(\cdot,\mathcal{D})} is non-trivial to compute. This is due to the nature of the encoding function 𝚝𝚘𝚔⇒​[𝒮]{\color[rgb]{1,0.4688,0.0781}\mathtt{tok}_{\Rightarrow}}[{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}\mathcal{S}}] used by top-down algorithms. Unlike in the bottom-up case, deleting a token here can change the preferred segmentation of an entire character-string, not only the local decomposition of the deleted token.88 8 For example, under a compression objective, suppose 𝒮=Σ∪{a​b​c,d​e​f,c​d​e​f}{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}\mathcal{S}}\!=\!{\color[rgb]{0.2734,0.4688,1}\Sigma}\cup\{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}abc},{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}def},{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}cdef}\}. Then, string a​b​c​d​e​f{\color[rgb]{0.2734,0.4688,1}abcdef} is segmented as ⟨a​b​c,d​e​f⟩{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}\langle abc,def\rangle}. If a​b​c{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}abc} is deleted, however, the shortest segmentation under the reduced vocabulary becomes ⟨a,b,c​d​e​f⟩{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}\langle a,b,cdef\rangle}, which also changes the previously used token d​e​f{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}def}. For the log-likelihood objective, the history gets worse. The segmentations produced by 𝚝𝚘𝚔⇒​[𝒮]{\color[rgb]{1,0.4688,0.0781}\mathtt{tok}_{\Rightarrow}}[{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}\mathcal{S}}] depend on p𝜽p_{\bm{\theta}}, which is itself estimated from the token counts. Deleting a token changes those counts, which changes p𝜽p_{\bm{\theta}}, which in turn changes how strings are segmented, which again changes the counts. Computing a deletion’s exact cost would thus require running this loop to convergence for each candidate token.

To approximate Δs𝔊⁡(⋅,𝒟)\Delta_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}}^{{\color[rgb]{1,0.4688,0.0781}\mathfrak{G}}(\cdot,\mathcal{D})}, we thus rely on a local replacement approximation: when scoring the deletion of s{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}, we keep the rest of the current model fixed and estimate the loss by only directly replacing occurrences of s{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s} with an alternative segmentation under 𝒮∖{s}{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}\mathcal{S}}\setminus\{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}\}.99 9 Note that this introduces an asymmetry between our two search procedures: the bottom-up merge gains in the previous section are exact, whereas the top-down deletion costs are only approximate. We emphasise that this asymmetry is not a design choice on our part, but an inherent property of top-down search procedures, being itself present in UnigramLM. We return to its implications in our Limitations section. For log-likelihood, this then yields the following result.

Lemma 3.

Under a local replacement approximation, the estimated increase in the negative log-likelihood objective due to deleting a token s∈𝒮∖Σ{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}\in{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}\mathcal{S}}\setminus{\color[rgb]{0.2734,0.4688,1}\Sigma} can be approximated as:1010 10 In practice, when computing this update, UnigramLM keeps segmentations latent and leverages p𝛉p_{\bm{\theta}} to compute nsDn_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}}^{{\lx@scalerel@obj{\mathcal{D}}}} as the expected count of s{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}, instead of its exact count under 𝚝𝚘𝚔⇒{\color[rgb]{1,0.4688,0.0781}\mathtt{tok}_{\Rightarrow}}.

Δs𝔊ll​(⋅,𝒟)≈nsD​(log⁡p𝜽​(s)−log⁡p𝜽​(𝐬srep)),\displaystyle\Delta_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}}^{{\color[rgb]{1,0.4688,0.0781}\mathfrak{G}}_{\mathrm{ll}}(\cdot,\mathcal{D})}\approx n_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}}^{{\lx@scalerel@obj{\mathcal{D}}}}\left(\log p_{\bm{\theta}}({\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s})-\log p_{\bm{\theta}}({\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}\mathbf{s}}^{\mathrm{rep}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}})\right), (11)

where p𝛉p_{\bm{\theta}} is the unigram model at step k−1k-1, and 𝐬srep{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}\mathbf{s}}^{\mathrm{rep}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}} is s{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}’s log-probability–optimal replacement segmentation, i.e., 𝐬srep=def𝚝𝚘𝚔⇒​[𝒮k−1∖{s}]​(s){\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}\mathbf{s}}^{\mathrm{rep}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\texttt{def}}}{{=}}{\color[rgb]{1,0.4688,0.0781}\mathtt{tok}_{\Rightarrow}}[{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}\mathcal{S}}_{k-1}\setminus\{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}\}]({\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}).

Proof sketch.

The full proof is in Appendix D. Before deletion, each expected occurrence of s{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s} contributes −log⁡p𝜽​(s)-\!\log p_{\bm{\theta}}({\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}) to the negative log-likelihood. Under the local replacement approximation, deleting s{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s} replaces it with 𝐬srep{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}\mathbf{s}}^{\mathrm{rep}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}}, which contributes −log⁡p𝜽​(𝐬srep)-\log p_{\bm{\theta}}({\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}\mathbf{s}}^{\mathrm{rep}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}}). As the number of such occurrences is nsDn_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}}^{{\lx@scalerel@obj{\mathcal{D}}}}, we get Eq. 11. ∎

After each deletion, we update our encoding function 𝚝𝚘𝚔⇒​[𝒮k]{\color[rgb]{1,0.4688,0.0781}\mathtt{tok}_{\Rightarrow}}[{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}\mathcal{S}}_{k}] by re-estimating p𝜽p_{\bm{\theta}}. We do this by updating 𝜽\bm{\theta} via an expectation–maximisation procedure, maximising the log-likelihood of 𝒟\mathcal{D}.1111 11 The details of this procedure fall out of our work’s scope; for an accessible derivation, see Meister (2026). This updated p𝜽p_{\bm{\theta}} defines the segmentations produced by 𝚝𝚘𝚔⇒{\color[rgb]{1,0.4688,0.0781}\mathtt{tok}_{\Rightarrow}}, which we use to re-segment our dataset. We now present an analogous update for compression.

Lemma 4.

Under a local replacement approximation, the estimated change in compression due to deleting a token s∈𝒮∖Σ{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}\in{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}\mathcal{S}}\setminus{\color[rgb]{0.2734,0.4688,1}\Sigma} can be approximated as:

Δs𝔊comp​(⋅,𝒟)=nsD​(|𝐬srep|−1),\displaystyle\Delta_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}}^{{\color[rgb]{1,0.4688,0.0781}\mathfrak{G}}_{\mathrm{comp}}(\cdot,\mathcal{D})}=n_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}}^{{\lx@scalerel@obj{\mathcal{D}}}}\left(|{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}\mathbf{s}}^{\mathrm{rep}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}}|-1\right), (12)

where 𝐬srep{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}\mathbf{s}}^{\mathrm{rep}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}} is the compression-optimal replacement of s{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s} after deletion: 𝐬srep=def𝚝𝚘𝚔⇒​[𝒮k−1∖{s}]​(s){\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}\mathbf{s}}^{\mathrm{rep}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\texttt{def}}}{{=}}{\color[rgb]{1,0.4688,0.0781}\mathtt{tok}_{\Rightarrow}}[{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}\mathcal{S}}_{k-1}\setminus\{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}\}]({\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}).

Proof sketch.

The full proof is in Appendix E. After deleting s{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}, the local replacement uses |𝐬srep||{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}\mathbf{s}}^{\mathrm{rep}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}}| tokens instead, thus increasing the corpus length by |𝐬srep|−1|{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}\mathbf{s}}^{\mathrm{rep}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}}|-1. There are nsDn_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}}^{{\lx@scalerel@obj{\mathcal{D}}}} such occurrences. ∎

Updating this compression-based tokeniser after a deletion is easier than for log-likelihood. No parameters need to be estimated: the vocabulary 𝒮k{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}\mathcal{S}}_{k} alone determines the encoding function, so we simply re-segment the corpus under 𝚝𝚘𝚔⇒​[𝒮k]{\color[rgb]{1,0.4688,0.0781}\mathtt{tok}_{\Rightarrow}}[{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}\mathcal{S}}_{k}].

5 Connection to Prior Work

As mentioned above, the tokenisation learning algorithms we propose are not entirely without precedent, and related to prior methods like WordPiece and PathPiece. In this section, we discuss this connections in detail.

5.1 BottomUpLL and Likelihood-Guided Merging

As noted in § 4.1, BottomUpLL favours pairs of tokens that are not only frequent, but which co-occur more often than chance. In fact, let the pointwise mutual information between two tokens be:

PMIadj⁡(s1,s2)\displaystyle\operatorname{PMI}_{\mathrm{adj}}({\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{1},{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{2}) =deflog⁡p𝜽​(s1,s2)p𝜽​(s1)​p𝜽​(s2)\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\texttt{def}}}{{=}}\log\frac{p_{\bm{\theta}}({\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{1},{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{2})}{p_{\bm{\theta}}({\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{1})\,p_{\bm{\theta}}({\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{2})} (13a)
=log⁡ND​ns1,s2Dns1D​ns2D.\displaystyle=\log\frac{N^{\lx@scalerel@obj{\mathcal{D}}}\,n_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{1},{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{2}}^{{\lx@scalerel@obj{\mathcal{D}}}}}{n_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{1}}^{{\lx@scalerel@obj{\mathcal{D}}}}n_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{2}}^{{\lx@scalerel@obj{\mathcal{D}}}}}. (13b)

Relying on the PMI to operationalise this notion of more-often-than-chance co-occurrence, we can use a Taylor approximation of Δs1,s2𝔊ll​(⋅,𝒟)\Delta_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{1},{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{2}}^{{\color[rgb]{1,0.4688,0.0781}\mathfrak{G}}_{\mathrm{ll}}(\cdot,\mathcal{D})} to make this explanation of BottomUpLL explicit.

Lemma 5.

Under a first-order Taylor approximation, the change in log-likelihood due to merging a token-pair can be approximated as:

Δs1,s2𝔊ll​(⋅,𝒟)≈ns1,s2D​(PMIadj⁡(s1,s2)−1).\displaystyle\Delta_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{1},{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{2}}^{{\color[rgb]{1,0.4688,0.0781}\mathfrak{G}}_{\mathrm{ll}}(\cdot,\mathcal{D})}\approx n_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{1},{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{2}}^{{\lx@scalerel@obj{\mathcal{D}}}}\left(\operatorname{PMI}_{\mathrm{adj}}({\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{1},{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{2})-1\right). (14)
Proof sketch.

The full proof is in Appendix F. Starting from Lemma 2, apply a first-order Taylor expansion independently to each x​log⁡xx\log x term. Collecting the resulting terms returns the equation above. ∎

Equation 14 is closely related to the objective of another famous bottom-up tokeniser, WordPiece. WordPiece’s definition, however, is far from unified and has shifted over time. As originally proposed by Schuster and Nakajima (2012), WordPiece selects the unit that most increases the likelihood of the data—i.e., using the same objective as BottomUpLL—but approximates the local objective, selecting multiple merges in parallel and only approximately updating their model p𝜽p_{\bm{\theta}}. WordPiece was later popularised by Wu et al. (2016), whose description suggests, in two consecutive sentences, optimising either a log-likelihood or a compression objective.1212 12 “The wordpiece model is generated using a data-driven approach to maximize the language-model likelihood of the training data […] Given a training corpus and a number of desired tokens DD, the optimization problem is to select DD wordpieces such that the resulting corpus is minimal in the number of wordpieces when segmented according to the chosen wordpiece model.” (Wu et al., 2016) Accordingly, the widely used HuggingFace implementation of WordPiece optimises for compression (Wolf et al., 2020). Finally, WordPiece is often described as merging the pair with the highest PMIadj\operatorname{PMI}_{\mathrm{adj}} (Schmidt et al., 2024; Lesci et al., 2025; Hugging Face, 2026), which relates to Eq. 14 but drops the ns1,s2Dn_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{1},{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{2}}^{{\lx@scalerel@obj{\mathcal{D}}}} factor. BottomUpLL is thus closest to the original WordPiece’s description, but differs from all existing versions of this method.

Importantly, even closer to Eq. 14 is S-BPE (Vilar and Federico, 2021), which scores merges by a count-weighted PMI criterion. The two expressions are not identical, as S-BPE omits the −1-1 term, but are otherwise equivalent. We experiment with a tokenisation learning algorithm based on Lemma 5 in some of our experiments, which we then label as BottomUpLL ≈\approx; when no such label is present, BottomUpLL refers to the method described by Lemma 2.

5.2 TopDownComp and Top-Down Compression

The closest prior method to TopDownComp is PathPiece (Schmidt et al., 2024), which likewise prunes a large initial vocabulary under a compression objective. The two differ in the deletion score: when scoring the removal of a token s{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}, PathPiece also considers re-segmentation of other vocabulary tokens that contain s{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s} as a substring, whereas TopDownComp considers only s{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}’s own local replacement. Adopting the PathPiece variant would change the algorithm in more ways than just the objective, so we keep TopDownComp as the direct compression counterpart of UnigramLM, differing from it in objective alone.

6 Experimental Setup

We will now compare our four tokenisers: BPE, BottomUpLL, TopDownComp, and UnigramLM. All four are trained with an identical preprocessing pipeline (NFC normalisation followed by a byte-level pretokeniser using the GPT-2 regex) and on the same corpus, so that any difference between them stems only from the objective and the search procedure. Appendix G gives the exact configuration under which we train our tokenisers. Full language model hyperparameter and architectural details are in Appendix H.

English setup.

For English experiments, we train our tokenisers on a subset with approximately 2B tokens from FineWeb-Edu (Lozhkov et al., 2024), using vocabulary sizes of 8k, 32k, and 128k. We then again use FineWeb-Edu to train language models using these tokenisers, evaluating 100M, 300M, 500M, and 1B parameter models.1313 13 Full hyperparameter and architectural details are in Appendix H. Results for 100M-parameter models are averaged over three random seeds, while larger models use one run per configuration. Finally, unless otherwise stated, models are trained with a Chinchilla-style token budget of approximately 20×20\times as many training tokens as model parameters.

Multilingual setup.

Our multilingual corpus contains 20B tokens across five languages: 10B English tokens from FineWeb-Edu (Lozhkov et al., 2024), and 2.5B tokens each of German, Spanish, Turkish, and Chinese from FineWeb2 (Penedo et al., 2025). We train our tokenisers on a 10% subsample of this corpus, using a single vocabulary size of 128k. We then train 1B-parameter language models on the full corpus.

Evaluation.

We report both extrinsic and intrinsic metrics. For extrinsic metrics, we report our language models’ bits per byte (BPB), computed on a held-out validation set, and minimal-pair grammatical accuracy, computed on BLiMP (Warstadt et al., 2020), MultiBLiMP (Jumelet et al., 2026), and ZhoBLiMP (Liu et al., 2026). For intrinsic metrics, we report 𝔊comp{\color[rgb]{1,0.4688,0.0781}\mathfrak{G}}_{\mathrm{comp}} and 𝔊ll{\color[rgb]{1,0.4688,0.0781}\mathfrak{G}}_{\mathrm{ll}}. We also report the unigram entropy of our tokenised corpus, its bytes per token (BPT), average vocab token len (Tok Len), vocabulary utilisation (Vocab Util), Zipf α\alpha, and Coverage 50%. Detailed definitions are in App. I.

7 Results

7.1 Intrinsic Evaluation

Compression vs. Log-likelihood.

Tab. 1 presents both the 𝔊comp{\color[rgb]{1,0.4688,0.0781}\mathfrak{G}}_{\mathrm{comp}} and 𝔊ll{\color[rgb]{1,0.4688,0.0781}\mathfrak{G}}_{\mathrm{ll}} achieved by our tokenisers. From this table, we can see that, for a small vocabulary (of 8​k8k tokens), the compression and log-likelihood scores achieved by the different tokenisers seem to align with their objective function: BPE and TopDownComp achieve better compression, while UnigramLM and BottomUpLL achieve better log-likelihood. For larger vocabularies, however, this surprisingly does not hold, with the bottom-up tokenisers consistently achieving both better compression and log-likelihood, irrespective of their objective function. Another result of interest is with respect to a tokeniser’s entropy, which, intuitively, measures how evenly a tokeniser spreads the frequency of its tokens. This quantity has a strong relationship to our optimisation objectives, which can be seen when we rewrite it:

Ent⁡(𝚝𝚘𝚔,𝒟)\displaystyle\mathrm{Ent}({\color[rgb]{1,0.4688,0.0781}\mathtt{tok}},\mathcal{D}) =def−∑s∈𝒮p𝜽(s)logp𝜽(s)\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\texttt{def}}}{{=}}-\sum_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}\in{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}\mathcal{S}}}p_{\bm{\theta}}({\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s})\log p_{\bm{\theta}}({\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}) (15a)
=𝔊ll​(𝚝𝚘𝚔,𝒟)𝔊comp​(𝚝𝚘𝚔,𝒟)\displaystyle=\frac{{\color[rgb]{1,0.4688,0.0781}\mathfrak{G}}_{\mathrm{ll}}({\color[rgb]{1,0.4688,0.0781}\mathtt{tok}},\mathcal{D})}{{\color[rgb]{1,0.4688,0.0781}\mathfrak{G}}_{\mathrm{comp}}({\color[rgb]{1,0.4688,0.0781}\mathtt{tok}},\mathcal{D})} (15b)

This follows directly from the definitions: writing p𝜽​(s)=nsD/NDp_{\bm{\theta}}({\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s})=n_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}}^{{\lx@scalerel@obj{\mathcal{D}}}}/N^{\lx@scalerel@obj{\mathcal{D}}}, and noting that NDN^{\lx@scalerel@obj{\mathcal{D}}}, the total number of tokens, is exactly 𝔊comp​(𝚝𝚘𝚔,𝒟){\color[rgb]{1,0.4688,0.0781}\mathfrak{G}}_{\mathrm{comp}}({\color[rgb]{1,0.4688,0.0781}\mathtt{tok}},\mathcal{D}), we get −∑sp𝜽(s)logp𝜽(s)=−1ND∑snsDlogp𝜽(s)=𝔊ll(𝚝𝚘𝚔,𝒟)/ND-\sum_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}}p_{\bm{\theta}}({\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s})\log p_{\bm{\theta}}({\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s})=-\frac{1}{N^{\lx@scalerel@obj{\mathcal{D}}}}\sum_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}}n_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}}^{{\lx@scalerel@obj{\mathcal{D}}}}\log p_{\bm{\theta}}({\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s})={\color[rgb]{1,0.4688,0.0781}\mathfrak{G}}_{\mathrm{ll}}({\color[rgb]{1,0.4688,0.0781}\mathtt{tok}},\mathcal{D})/N^{\lx@scalerel@obj{\mathcal{D}}}. Looking at the entropy values in Tab. 1 we see a similar behaviour as before: for small vocabularies, entropy results align with the choice of tokenisation objective; for a larger vocabulary, however, top-down methods achieve consistently lower entropy. Future work should further investigate this relationship between objective and search procedure.

Distributional Properties of Tokens.

Table 1 also reports our tokenisers’ Zipf α\alpha and Coverage 50%, where Zipf α\alpha is the negated slope of a frequency vs. rank log-log curve, and Coverage 50% is the smallest ℓ\ell such that the ℓ\ell most frequent tokens together account for at least half of all token occurrences in our corpus. A larger Zipf α\alpha thus means that token frequency decreases more rapidly with rank, while lower Coverage 50% values indicate that token occurrences are concentrated among fewer token types. Figure 2 shows corresponding frequency–rank curves. Within each search family, the likelihood-based method induces a more concentrated token-frequency distribution than the compression-based method: BottomUpLL has higher Zipf α\alpha, lower entropy, and lower Coverage 50% than BPE, and UnigramLM shows the same pattern relative to TopDownComp. Thus, while the search procedure may dictate the values of 𝔊comp{\color[rgb]{1,0.4688,0.0781}\mathfrak{G}}_{\mathrm{comp}} and 𝔊ll{\color[rgb]{1,0.4688,0.0781}\mathfrak{G}}_{\mathrm{ll}}, the used objective is still visible in a tokenised corpus’ empirical token-frequency distribution.

Other Intrinsic Metrics.

Finally, Tab. 1 also presents our tokenisers’ vocabulary utilisation—i.e., the proportion of vocabulary items used at least once on a test set of 47,384 documents—as well as the average length of the tokens in their vocabularies. Vocabulary utilisation is close to 100% at 8k and 32k, but at 128k, likelihood-based tokenisers have more unused tokens; Appendix K traces this to the intermediate tokens that BottomUpLL creates during merging and then never uses again. Token length behaves differently across vocabulary sizes: at small vocabulary sizes, top-down methods present longer tokens, as they can retain these tokens from the initial seed vocabulary; at larger vocabulary sizes, though, bottom-up methods present longer tokens instead, as they can build these tokens from scratch through successive merges. Interestingly, across both search procedures, the likelihood-based tokenisers have longer tokens than their compression-based counterparts.

Vocabulary Composition.

We now move on to analysing the composition of our tokenisers’ vocabularies. To this end, we compute their similarity, defined as |𝒮A∩𝒮B|/|𝒮A|\nicefrac{{|{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}\mathcal{S}}_{A}\cap{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}\mathcal{S}}_{B}|}}{{|{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}\mathcal{S}}_{A}|}}. Figure 3 presents these results. From this table, we see that learned vocabularies cluster primarily by search procedure: e.g., bottom-up methods share substantially more tokens with each other than with top-down methods. This indicates that a tokeniser’s search procedure has a large effect on which tokens are included in its final vocabulary. Figure 4 in Appendix L shows the full set-overlap structure of all five vocabularies. Furthermore, per-example qualitative segmentations for the four tokenisers are shown in Appendix M.

7.2 Extrinsic Evaluation

BPB.

Tables 2 and 3 present extrinsic results for both the English and multilingual settings. From these tables, we can see that bottom-up tokenisers consistently achieve lower BPB scores than top-down. This holds true for all our experimental conditions, with the only exception of the English 300M models at 32k vocabulary, where TopDownComp outperforms BPE by a negligible margin (0.00030.0003 BPB); the likelihood-based pair (BottomUpLL vs. UnigramLM) favours bottom-up in every setting.1414 14 Because several of these differences are small, we additionally verify their significance with a paired document-level bootstrap over the evaluation set, which confirms the statistical significance of each of these comparisons (see details in Appendix N). Comparing tokenisers within a single search procedure, we see that the choice of objective is still relevant, albeit less strongly. Compression-based methods tend to outperform log-likelihood; but there are several exceptions where BottomUpLL outperforms all other methods.

Minimal-pair accuracy.

Tables 2 and 3 also present scores on a minimal-pair grammaticality task, for both the English and multilingual settings. Notably, these results do not show the same clear preference as BPB for bottom-up over top-down. In fact, in the English setting, top-down methods often outperform the bottom-up ones, with UnigramLM outperforming BottomUpLL and TopDownComp outperforming BPE for the 1B models. In the multilingual setting, no consistent pattern arises either, and all tokenisers perform best in at least one language. Our results in German, Spanish, and Turkish, however, suggest that top-down methods may be helpful for morphologically rich languages. More broadly, our multilingual minimal-pair accuracy results suggest different tokenisers induce different inductive biases, which will in turn be uniquely suited to different languages; we leave this direction to future work.

8 Conclusion

Our paper disentangles two important design choices in tokeniser learning algorithms: the objective used to score a tokeniser and the search procedure used to optimise it. We analyse two objectives (compression vs. log-likelihood) and search procedures (bottom-up vs. top-down), introducing two new tokenisers in the process: BottomUpLL and TopDownComp. In nearly all experimental conditions, language models trained with bottom-up tokenisers outperformed top-down ones in terms of bits-per-byte. Our intrinsic evaluations also highlighted a surprising pattern: bottom-up tokenisers produced both more compressed and higher log-likelihood token-strings than top-down tokenisers, independent of the used objective function. The used objective still affects the resulting tokeniser, though, with log-likelihood objective leaving a clear impact on the empirical rank--frequency distribution of its tokens. Overall, our results show that a tokeniser’s effect on language modelling cannot be explained by the objective alone, and that the used search procedure is an important component of tokeniser design. We hope future work will explore the impact of other optimisation objectives and search procedures1515 15 Investigating the search procedures of, e.g.,Tempus et al. (2026) or Chizhov et al. (2024). in language modelling.

Limitations

We list a few limitations with our study here.

Scale.

First, we only train language models up to 1B parameters, and results could shift for larger models or longer training horizons.

Languages.

Second, our multilingual experiments cover five selected languages: English, German, Spanish, Turkish, and Chinese. Four of these use the Latin script and all are relatively high-resource, so our multilingual results should be read as applying to these five languages rather than to multilingual tokenisation in general. How our findings transfer to low-resource languages, and to scripts with markedly different orthographic conventions, remains an open question that we leave to future work.

Single seed at scale.

Third, for computational reasons, the 300M and 500M models are trained with a single seed per configuration, as are the multilingual 1B models; the 100M and English 1B models are averaged over three seeds; small differences in results across tokenisers should thus be interpreted with caution.

Tokeniser-training corpus.

Fourth, in all our experiments, each tokeniser is trained on the same corpus as the language model trained on top of it. We thus do not analyse the impact of training models on data that differ in domain or style from its tokeniser.

Approximate top-down deletion scores.

Fifth, as discussed in § 4.2, top-down deletion costs rely on the local replacement approximation, whereas bottom-up merge gains are exact for the current step. We asses the impact of this approximation by, at a small scale, training tokenisers for which we compute exact deletion scoring. We find that the local-replacement-approximation tokenisers present an 81.5%81.5\% vocabulary overlap with these exact ones. Whether this holds at the vocabulary sizes used in our main experiments, however, remains open. A second approximation we rely on for top-down methods is that we prune multiple tokens per round rather than one at a time. We assess the impact of this approximation by re-training the top-down tokenisers with pruning rates of 1%1\% and 0.1%0.1\% of the vocabulary per round, instead of the 10%10\% used in our main experiments: the resulting vocabularies overlap with the 10%10\% ones by over 97%97\% for UnigramLM and over 99%99\% for TopDownComp, suggesting that this approximation has a limited effect on the learned vocabulary. Details for both experiments are in Appendix O.

Evaluation.

Finally, we evaluate models with BPB and minimal-pair grammatical benchmarks (BLiMP, MultiBLiMP, ZhoBLiMP). We do not measure other downstream task performance, reasoning ability, or long-context behaviour; how our models perform in those different settings is thus left open.

Appendix B Updating Counts in bottom-up Procedures

Both BPE and BottomUpLL repeatedly select a token-pair based on its merge gain on the current tokenised corpus. A naive implementation would recompute token and token-pair counts after each merge, which is expensive on large corpora. Instead, our implementation maintains these counts incrementally and updates only the parts of the corpus affected by the selected merge.

The corpus is represented as a collection of unique word types, each with an associated frequency. Each word type stores its current tokenisation using a linked token structure: every token stores pointers to its predecessor and successor, allowing merges to be applied locally without reconstructing the full token string. We maintain a mapping

pair​_​to​_​words:⟨s1,s2⟩\displaystyle\mathrm{pair\_to\_words}:\langle{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{1},{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{2}\rangle (18)
↦{word types containing ​⟨s1,s2⟩},\displaystyle\qquad\mapsto\{\text{word types containing }\langle{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{1},{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{2}\rangle\},

which maps each token-pair to the word types in which that pair currently occurs. We also maintain a reverse index from tokens to the token-pairs containing them, which allows us to identify which candidate scores may be affected after a merge.

When a merge m=⟨s1,s2⟩{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}m}=\langle{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{1},{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{2}\rangle is selected, write

snew=defs1∘s2.{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{\mathrm{new}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\texttt{def}}}{{=}}{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{1}\circ{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{2}.

Each affected word type is scanned through its linked token sequence, and non-overlapping occurrences of ⟨s1,s2⟩\langle{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{1},{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{2}\rangle are replaced by snew{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{\mathrm{new}}. The non-overlap condition is enforced during this scan: once an occurrence has been merged, the scan skips over the newly created token, so overlapping occurrences of the same pair are not counted twice.

Locally, an occurrence in context

⟨sℓ,s1,s2,sr⟩\displaystyle\langle{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{\ell},{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{1},{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{2},{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{r}\rangle (19)

is replaced by

⟨sℓ,snew,sr⟩,\displaystyle\langle{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{\ell},{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{\mathrm{new}},{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{r}\rangle, (20)

where sℓ{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{\ell} and sr{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{r} denote the immediate left and right neighbours, if they exist. Therefore, only token-pairs in this local neighbourhood can change. The old token-pairs

⟨sℓ,s1⟩,⟨s1,s2⟩,⟨s2,sr⟩\displaystyle\langle{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{\ell},{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{1}\rangle,\qquad\langle{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{1},{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{2}\rangle,\qquad\langle{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{2},{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{r}\rangle (21)

are removed, and the new token-pairs

⟨sℓ,snew⟩,⟨snew,sr⟩\displaystyle\langle{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{\ell},{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{\mathrm{new}}\rangle,\qquad\langle{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{\mathrm{new}},{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{r}\rangle (22)

are added. Boundary cases are handled by omitting updates involving missing neighbours.

For one merged occurrence, the affected pair counts are updated as

nsℓ,s1D\displaystyle n_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{\ell},{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{1}}^{{\lx@scalerel@obj{\mathcal{D}}}} ←nsℓ,s1D−1,\displaystyle\leftarrow n_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{\ell},{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{1}}^{{\lx@scalerel@obj{\mathcal{D}}}}-1, (23a)
ns1,s2D\displaystyle n_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{1},{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{2}}^{{\lx@scalerel@obj{\mathcal{D}}}} ←ns1,s2D−1,\displaystyle\leftarrow n_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{1},{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{2}}^{{\lx@scalerel@obj{\mathcal{D}}}}-1, (23b)
ns2,srD\displaystyle n_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{2},{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{r}}^{{\lx@scalerel@obj{\mathcal{D}}}} ←ns2,srD−1,\displaystyle\leftarrow n_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{2},{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{r}}^{{\lx@scalerel@obj{\mathcal{D}}}}-1, (23c)
nsℓ,snewD\displaystyle n_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{\ell},{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{\mathrm{new}}}^{{\lx@scalerel@obj{\mathcal{D}}}} ←nsℓ,snewD+1,\displaystyle\leftarrow n_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{\ell},{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{\mathrm{new}}}^{{\lx@scalerel@obj{\mathcal{D}}}}+1, (23d)
nsnew,srD\displaystyle n_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{\mathrm{new}},{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{r}}^{{\lx@scalerel@obj{\mathcal{D}}}} ←nsnew,srD+1.\displaystyle\leftarrow n_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{\mathrm{new}},{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{r}}^{{\lx@scalerel@obj{\mathcal{D}}}}+1. (23e)

When word types have frequencies, these increments and decrements are weighted by the corresponding word-type frequency.

For BottomUpLL, we also update unigram counts, since the merge score in Lemma 2 depends on both token counts and pair counts. If ns1,s2Dn_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{1},{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{2}}^{{\lx@scalerel@obj{\mathcal{D}}}} denotes the frequency-weighted number of non-overlapping occurrences of the selected pair that are actually merged, then the unigram counts are updated as

ns1D\displaystyle n_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{1}}^{{\lx@scalerel@obj{\mathcal{D}}}} ←ns1D−ns1,s2D,\displaystyle\leftarrow n_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{1}}^{{\lx@scalerel@obj{\mathcal{D}}}}-n_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{1},{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{2}}^{{\lx@scalerel@obj{\mathcal{D}}}}, (24a)
ns2D\displaystyle n_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{2}}^{{\lx@scalerel@obj{\mathcal{D}}}} ←ns2D−ns1,s2D,\displaystyle\leftarrow n_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{2}}^{{\lx@scalerel@obj{\mathcal{D}}}}-n_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{1},{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{2}}^{{\lx@scalerel@obj{\mathcal{D}}}}, (24b)
nsnewD\displaystyle n_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{\mathrm{new}}}^{{\lx@scalerel@obj{\mathcal{D}}}} ←ns1,s2D,\displaystyle\leftarrow n_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{1},{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{2}}^{{\lx@scalerel@obj{\mathcal{D}}}}, (24c)
ND\displaystyle N^{\lx@scalerel@obj{\mathcal{D}}} ←ND−ns1,s2D.\displaystyle\leftarrow N^{\lx@scalerel@obj{\mathcal{D}}}-n_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{1},{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}^{2}}^{{\lx@scalerel@obj{\mathcal{D}}}}. (24d)

For BPE, the affected candidate scores are simply the updated pair counts, as in Lemma 1. For BottomUpLL, affected candidate scores are then recomputed using the local likelihood-change expression in Lemma 2.

The priority queue of candidate token-pairs is maintained lazily. After a merge, the selected pair is removed from the pair-to-word index, affected reverse-index entries are updated, and affected token-pairs are pushed back onto the heap with fresh scores. Old heap entries are not removed immediately. Instead, stale entries are rejected when popped: the implementation checks the current count and score, and discards the heap entry if it no longer matches the current state. The heap is also periodically rebuilt to control the accumulation of stale entries.

This gives an incremental implementation in which the cost of a merge is proportional to the number of affected word types and local token updates, plus the cost of heap maintenance. In practice, this is much cheaper than recomputing all token and token-pair counts over the full corpus after every merge.

Appendix C Proof of Lemma 2

See 2

Proof.

We prove the result by explicitly writing the corpus log-likelihood before and after applying the merge. Let the current tokenised corpus contain NDN^{\lx@scalerel@obj{\mathcal{D}}} tokens in total. For each token s~\tilde{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}}, let ns~Dn_{\tilde{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}}}^{{\lx@scalerel@obj{\mathcal{D}}}} denote its corpus count. Under the unigram token model, the empirical probability of s~\tilde{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}} is

p𝜽​(s~)=ns~DND.\displaystyle p_{\bm{\theta}}(\tilde{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}})=\frac{n_{\tilde{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}}}^{{\lx@scalerel@obj{\mathcal{D}}}}}{N^{\lx@scalerel@obj{\mathcal{D}}}}. (25)

Therefore, the corpus log-likelihood before applying the merge is

Appendix D Proof of Lemma 3

See 3

Proof.

We prove the result under the local replacement approximation stated in the lemma. That is, when scoring the deletion of s{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}, we keep the current token probabilities p𝜽p_{\bm{\theta}} fixed, keep all other segmentation decisions fixed, and approximate the effect of deletion by replacing each expected occurrence of s{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s} with a replacement segmentation under 𝒮∖{s}{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}\mathcal{S}}\setminus\{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}\}.

For UnigramLM, token usage is measured by expected counts under the current posterior over valid segmentations. Thus, nsDn_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}}^{{\lx@scalerel@obj{\mathcal{D}}}} is the expected number of times s{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s} is used in the corpus. Before deleting s{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}, each such expected occurrence contributes

−log⁡p𝜽​(s)\displaystyle-\log p_{\bm{\theta}}({\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}) (32)

to the negative log-likelihood objective.

After deleting s{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}, the token can no longer be used as a single token. Under the local replacement approximation, each occurrence of s{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s} is replaced by the highest-probability valid segmentation of the same string under the reduced vocabulary:

𝐬srep=defargmax𝐬~∈(𝒮∖{s})∗s​=∘​𝐬~p𝜽​(𝐬~).\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}\mathbf{s}}^{\mathrm{rep}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\texttt{def}}}{{=}}\argmax_{\begin{subarray}{c}\tilde{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}\mathbf{s}}}\in({\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}\mathcal{S}}\setminus\{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}\})^{*}\\ {\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}\overset{\circ}{=}\tilde{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}\mathbf{s}}}\end{subarray}}p_{\bm{\theta}}(\tilde{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}\mathbf{s}}}). (33)

Since p𝜽p_{\bm{\theta}} is a unigram model, the probability of this replacement token-string is

p𝜽​(𝐬srep)=∏s~∈𝐬srepp𝜽​(s~).\displaystyle p_{\bm{\theta}}({\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}\mathbf{s}}^{\mathrm{rep}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}})=\prod_{\tilde{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}}\in{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}\mathbf{s}}^{\mathrm{rep}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}}}p_{\bm{\theta}}(\tilde{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}}). (34)

After replacement, each expected occurrence therefore contributes

−log⁡p𝜽​(𝐬srep)\displaystyle-\log p_{\bm{\theta}}({\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}\mathbf{s}}^{\mathrm{rep}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}}) (35)

to the negative log-likelihood objective.

Hence, the estimated increase in negative log-likelihood for one expected occurrence of s{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s} is

−log⁡p𝜽​(𝐬srep)−(−log⁡p𝜽​(s))\displaystyle-\log p_{\bm{\theta}}({\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}\mathbf{s}}^{\mathrm{rep}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}})-\bigl(-\log p_{\bm{\theta}}({\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s})\bigr)
=log⁡p𝜽​(s)−log⁡p𝜽​(𝐬srep).\displaystyle\qquad=\log p_{\bm{\theta}}({\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s})-\log p_{\bm{\theta}}({\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}\mathbf{s}}^{\mathrm{rep}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}}). (36)

Multiplying this per-occurrence increase by the expected number of occurrences nsDn_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}}^{{\lx@scalerel@obj{\mathcal{D}}}} gives

Δs𝔊ll​(⋅,𝒟)≈nsD​(log⁡p𝜽​(s)−log⁡p𝜽​(𝐬srep)).\displaystyle\Delta_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}}^{{\color[rgb]{1,0.4688,0.0781}\mathfrak{G}}_{\mathrm{ll}}(\cdot,\mathcal{D})}\approx n_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}}^{{\lx@scalerel@obj{\mathcal{D}}}}\left(\log p_{\bm{\theta}}({\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s})-\log p_{\bm{\theta}}({\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}\mathbf{s}}^{\mathrm{rep}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.8633,0.1953,0.5508}s}})\right). (37)
